title: Containers with Docker
text:
All course scripts are meant to run inside the Docker image that contains the required tool. The script contains the analysis logic; the Docker command only chooses the software environment and mounts the project folder:
docker run --rm \
  --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$PWD:/work" \
  -w /work \
  docker.io/fgualdr/ngs-fastqc:latest \
  bash scripts/day1/01_fastqc_raw.sh

title: Containers with Docker
text:
Why this matters
The image provides software. The mounted project folder provides persistent files. docker run --rm starts a temporary container, runs the script inside /work, writes outputs into the mounted project folder, and removes the container when the command finishes. This separation makes the analysis portable across macOS, Linux, and Windows WSL2.

title: Containers with Docker
text:
Practical limits
Use two threads by default:
THREADS=2
More threads can overload student laptops and make failures harder to debug.

title: Day 0 - Technical setup for a reproducible NGS workshop
text:
2. Software installation
Install or verify the software below before the workshop. These are the applications and command-line tools that students will actually use during the course.








Software
What it is used for
Practical note for this workshop




Visual Studio Code
Editing scripts, notes, configuration files, and Markdown/Quarto files.
Main editor for the workshop. Windows users should open the project through the WSL extension.


Docker
Running container images that contain the bioinformatics software.
Docker is the supported route for the practical scripts.


Git
Tracking project changes and synchronizing the repository with GitHub.
Required for the student analysis repository created on Day 1.


IGV
Visual inspection of aligned reads, coverage tracks, and genomic regions.
Required for genome-browser inspection exercises.




Supported installation routes
Use the route for your operating system. Windows users need an Ubuntu Linux environment through WSL2 so that workshop commands run in a Linux shell while Docker Desktop provides the container engine. macOS users will use Homebrew where possible to simplify command-line tool installation and checks.



Operating system
Supported route




Windows 10/11
WSL2 + Ubuntu + Docker Desktop with WSL2 integration


macOS
VS Code + Homebrew + Docker Desktop for Mac


Linux
Docker Engine



Jump directly to your operating system:

Windows 10/11 setup
macOS setup
Linux setup

Do not install multiple container engines for this workshop unless you already know what you are doing. One working Docker installation is enough.


Docker Desktop licensing
Docker Desktop is free for educational use under Docker’s current subscription terms. In this workshop, Docker Desktop is used for teaching and learning in a university context.
If you are using your own laptop, Docker Desktop is the recommended route. If you are using an institutionally managed computer, check whether your institution has specific Docker Desktop installation or licensing rules.
Useful reference: Docker Desktop subscription terms


2.1 Windows 10/11
The supported Windows route is:
Windows 10/11 -> WSL2 Ubuntu -> Docker Desktop with WSL2 integration -> VS Code connected to WSL -> IGV
The goal is to run all workshop commands from an Ubuntu Linux terminal, opened inside Visual Studio Code.
Windows will still be used for desktop applications such as Docker Desktop, Visual Studio Code, and IGV. The command-line analysis will run inside Ubuntu through WSL2.








Component
Where it runs
What it does




Visual Studio Code
Windows
The editor application.


WSL extension for VS Code
Windows and WSL
Lets VS Code open files and terminals inside Ubuntu.


Ubuntu WSL2
Linux environment inside Windows
The place where workshop shell commands run.


Docker Desktop
Windows, integrated with WSL2
Provides the docker command inside Ubuntu.


IGV Desktop
Windows
Genome browser used for visual inspection.



Do not run workshop commands from PowerShell, CMD, Git Bash, Anaconda Prompt, or a normal Windows terminal after setup. Use the VS Code terminal connected to Ubuntu WSL.
The workshop project should be created inside the Ubuntu filesystem:
~/workshop_ngs
Do not create the workshop project under:
/mnt/c/...
This avoids common path, permission, mount, and file-speed problems.
Also avoid OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud Drive, network-mounted folders, and paths with spaces for the main workshop project. These locations can cause slow file access, permission problems, and Docker mount errors.

Step 1: install WSL2 and Ubuntu
Open Windows Terminal or PowerShell as administrator.
Run:
wsl --install
This installs WSL and the default Ubuntu distribution. If this command is not available or does not work on your computer, follow the official Microsoft WSL installation instructions.
If Windows asks you to restart, restart the computer.
After restart, Ubuntu may open automatically. If not, open Ubuntu from the Windows Start menu. (Look for the Linux penguin icon)
The first time Ubuntu starts, it will ask you to create:

a Linux username;
a Linux password.

This password is used for Ubuntu commands such as sudo. It is not your Windows password and it is not your GitHub password.


Step 2: check that Ubuntu uses WSL2
Open Windows Terminal or PowerShell and check that Ubuntu is using WSL2:
wsl -l -v
Expected output:
  NAME      STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu    Running         2
If Ubuntu shows version 1, ask for help before continuing.


Step 3: update Ubuntu and install basic command-line tools
Open Ubuntu from the Windows Start menu.
Run:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y git gawk curl wget ca-certificates unzip
Check Git:
git --version
Expected output:
git version 2.x.x
The exact version number may be different.


Step 4: install Docker Desktop for Windows
Install Docker Desktop for Windows. Depending on which version of Windows you are using, Docker Desktop may prompt you to turn on WSL 2 during installation. Read the information displayed on the screen and turn on the WSL 2 feature to continue.
Open Docker Desktop after installation.
In Docker Desktop settings:

Go to Settings -> General.
Make sure Use the WSL 2 based engine
Go to Resources -> WSL integration.
Enable integration with Ubuntu.
Click Apply & restart if requested.



Step 5: test Docker from Ubuntu
Open the Ubuntu terminal.
Run:
docker --version
docker run --rm hello-world
The first time you run this command, Docker may first download the small hello-world image. Output similar to this is normal:
Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally
latest: Pulling from library/hello-world
...
Status: Downloaded newer image for hello-world:latest

Hello from Docker!
This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.
The exact digest, platform, and download details may be different.
This confirms that Docker Desktop is correctly connected to Ubuntu WSL.
If docker is not found, open Docker Desktop settings again and check:
Resources -> WSL integration -> Ubuntu enabled


Step 6: install Visual Studio Code
Install Visual Studio Code for Windows.
Open Visual Studio Code once after installation.


Step 7: install the WSL extension in VS Code
In Visual Studio Code:
Extensions -> search "WSL" -> install "WSL" by Microsoft
Useful reference: Use WSL in Visual Studio Code


Step 8: connect VS Code to Ubuntu WSL
In Visual Studio Code, use:
Ctrl + Shift + P -> WSL: Connect to WSL
or:
Remote Explorer -> WSL -> Ubuntu
Open a new terminal:
Terminal -> New Terminal
The terminal should show a Linux-style prompt, for example:
your_username@computer_name:~$
Check:
pwd
Expected output:
/home/your_username
If the prompt looks like this:
PS C:\Users\your_username>
you are still in a Windows terminal. Reconnect VS Code to WSL before continuing.


Step 9: create the workshop folder inside Ubuntu
In the VS Code terminal connected to Ubuntu WSL, run:
mkdir -p ~/workshop_ngs
cd ~/workshop_ngs
pwd
Expected output:
/home/your_username/workshop_ngs
Open this folder in VS Code:
code .
If VS Code asks whether to reopen the folder in WSL, accept.
After this, the Explorer panel should show the workshop_ngs folder, and the terminal should still show a Linux-style prompt.


Step 10: open the Ubuntu folder from Windows Explorer
Keep the workshop project inside Ubuntu WSL. This is the safest location for Linux commands, Git, Docker mounts, and file permissions.
You can still browse the same folder with normal Windows clicks when you need to open a table, HTML report, PDF, or image with a Windows program such as Excel, Edge, or IGV.
From the VS Code terminal connected to Ubuntu WSL, run:
explorer.exe .
Windows File Explorer will open the current Ubuntu folder. You will be able to double-click small output files from there, like those we will generate under the folders:
raw_data/metadata/*.csv
results/day1_qc/fastqc_raw/*_fastqc.html
results/day2_rnaseq/counts/*.tsv
results/day2_rnaseq/deseq2/*.csv
You can also paste this kind of path into the Windows Explorer address bar:
\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\your_username\workshop_ngs
If your Ubuntu distribution has a slightly different name, open Windows Explorer and type:
\\wsl.localhost\
Then click into the Ubuntu distribution, then home, then your username, then workshop_ngs.
Important rule: use Windows Explorer for browsing and opening results, but run workshop commands from the VS Code terminal connected to Ubuntu WSL.


Step 11: test folder mounting with Docker
In the VS Code terminal connected to Ubuntu WSL, first move into the workshop setup folder:
cd ~/workshop_ngs
mkdir -p test_mount
echo "Docker can read this file" > test_mount/message.txt
Then run:
docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD/test_mount:/work" \
  alpine:latest \
  cat /work/message.txt
Expected output:
Docker can read this file
This confirms that Docker can mount a folder from the Ubuntu WSL project directory into a container.


Step 12: install IGV on Windows
Install IGV Desktop on Windows.
Open IGV once to confirm that it starts correctly.



2.2 macOS
The supported macOS route is:
macOS -> VS Code -> Homebrew -> Git/basic tools -> Docker Desktop -> IGV
The goal is to open the workshop folder in Visual Studio Code and run all commands from the VS Code terminal or the macOS Terminal.

Step 1: install Visual Studio Code
Install Visual Studio Code for macOS.
Open Visual Studio Code once to confirm that it starts correctly.


Step 2: install Homebrew
Homebrew is a package manager for macOS. It will be used to install or check command-line tools.
In Terminal, run the installer command from the official Homebrew page:
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
If the installer prints additional commands under Next steps, run those commands in the same Terminal window so that brew is available on your PATH.
After installation, open Terminal and check:
brew --version
Expected output:
Homebrew x.x.x
The exact version number may be different.


Step 3: install Git and basic command-line tools
In Terminal, run:
brew install git curl wget
Check Git:
git --version
Expected output:
git version 2.x.x
The exact version number may be different.


Step 4: install Docker Desktop for Mac
Install Docker Desktop for Mac.
After installation, open Docker Desktop and wait until Docker reports that it is running.
Check Docker from Terminal or from the VS Code terminal:
docker --version
docker run --rm hello-world
The first time you run this command, Docker may first download the small hello-world image. Output similar to this is normal:
Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally
latest: Pulling from library/hello-world
...
Status: Downloaded newer image for hello-world:latest

Hello from Docker!
This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.
The exact digest, platform, and download details may be different.
This confirms that Docker can download and run a container image.


Step 5: create the workshop folder
Create a simple workshop folder in your home directory:
mkdir -p ~/workshop_ngs
cd ~/workshop_ngs
pwd
Expected output:
/Users/your_username/workshop_ngs
Avoid iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, network-mounted folders, and paths with spaces for the main workshop project. A simple folder directly under your home directory is safer for Git, Docker mounts, and command-line paths.
Open this folder in Visual Studio Code:
code .
If the code command is not available, open Visual Studio Code manually and use:
File -> Open Folder
Then select the workshop_ngs folder.


Step 6: test folder mounting with Docker
From the VS Code terminal or macOS Terminal, first move into the workshop setup folder:
cd ~/workshop_ngs
mkdir -p test_mount
echo "Docker can read this file" > test_mount/message.txt
Then run:
docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD/test_mount:/work" \
  alpine:latest \
  cat /work/message.txt
Expected output:
Docker can read this file
This confirms that Docker can mount a local project folder inside a container.


Step 7: install IGV
Install IGV Desktop.
Alternatively, if Homebrew is working, IGV can be installed with:
brew install --cask igv-desktop
Open IGV once to confirm that it starts correctly.



2.3 Linux
The supported Linux route is:
Linux -> VS Code -> Git/basic tools -> Docker Engine -> IGV
Linux students should use the normal Linux terminal or the VS Code terminal opened from the workshop project folder.
Homebrew is not required on Linux for this workshop. Use the normal package manager for your Linux distribution.
The tools required on Linux are:







Tool
Purpose




Git
Track changes and synchronize the repository with GitHub.


curl
Download files and query web resources from the command line.


wget
Download files from URLs.


ca-certificates
Allow secure HTTPS downloads.


unzip
Extract compressed archives when needed.


Docker Engine
Run containerized bioinformatics tools.


Visual Studio Code
Edit scripts, notes, and configuration files.


IGV
Inspect genome-aligned sequencing data.




Step 1: install Visual Studio Code
Install Visual Studio Code for Linux.
Open Visual Studio Code once to confirm that it starts correctly.


Step 2: install Git and basic command-line tools
On Ubuntu or Debian-based Linux distributions, open a terminal and run:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git curl wget ca-certificates unzip
Check Git:
git --version
Expected output:
git version 2.x.x
The exact version number may be different.
For other Linux distributions, install the same tools using your distribution package manager.


Step 3: install Docker Engine
For Ubuntu, follow the official Docker Engine installation instructions for Ubuntu.
For other Linux distributions, use the corresponding official Docker Engine installation page.
Use the page matching your Linux distribution.


Step 4: check Docker
After installation, check Docker:
docker --version
Then run the test container:
docker run --rm hello-world
The first time you run this command, Docker may first download the small hello-world image. Output similar to this is normal:
Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally
latest: Pulling from library/hello-world
...
Status: Downloaded newer image for hello-world:latest

Hello from Docker!
This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.
The exact digest, platform, and download details may be different.
If Docker reports a permission error, try:
sudo docker run --rm hello-world
If this works only with sudo, your user does not yet have permission to access the Docker daemon. Follow Docker’s Linux post-installation instructions or ask for help before the workshop.


Step 5: create the workshop folder
Create a simple workshop folder in your home directory:
mkdir -p ~/workshop_ngs
cd ~/workshop_ngs
pwd
Expected output:
/home/your_username/workshop_ngs
Avoid network-mounted folders, synchronized cloud folders such as Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud Drive, and paths with spaces for the main workshop project.
Open this folder in Visual Studio Code:
code .
If the code command is not available, open Visual Studio Code manually and use:
File -> Open Folder
Then select the workshop_ngs folder.


Step 6: test folder mounting with Docker
From the VS Code terminal or Linux terminal, first move into the workshop setup folder:
cd ~/workshop_ngs
mkdir -p test_mount
echo "Docker can read this file" > test_mount/message.txt
Then run:
docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD/test_mount:/work" \
  alpine:latest \
  cat /work/message.txt
Expected output:
Docker can read this file
This confirms that Docker can mount a local project folder inside a container.


Step 7: install IGV
Install IGV Desktop.
Open IGV once to confirm that it starts correctly.

You can log in to GitHub.

title: Reproducible NGS Data Analysis
text:
Welcome
Modern sequencing projects require much more than running bioinformatics tools.
A reproducible analysis requires:
metadata retrieval
-> raw data retrieval
-> workflow execution
-> design-specific analysis
-> documentation
-> version control
This workshop introduces a practical workflow for organizing, executing, documenting, and interpreting RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses using public datasets and lightweight computational infrastructure.
The practical examples focus on bacterial genomes and small datasets that can be explored on personal laptops, while introducing concepts that can also scale to larger projects and institutional computing environments.






Important



This workshop teaches a reproducible approach to RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analysis using public sequencing datasets, containers, Git/GitHub, and structured project documentation.
Rather than focusing on a single software package, the workshop emphasizes workflows that can be understood, reproduced, shared, and adapted to real research projects.
The goal is to give you practical experience with the core steps of reference-based NGS analysis and to provide a project framework that you can reuse in your own research or laboratory work.





Learning objectives
By the end of the workshop, you should be able to:

Create a reproducible NGS project structure
Use Git and GitHub to document analyses
Use Docker containers to run bioinformatics tools
Retrieve public sequencing datasets from SRA, ENA, and ArrayExpress
Generate and interpret quality-control reports
Perform basic RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses
Produce differential expression and peak-calling results
Associate regulatory regions with nearby genes
Document and communicate results through reports and figures




Workshop structure







Day
Main topic




Day 0
Setup and readiness


Day 1
Reproducible project setup, FASTQ QC/trimming, and reference files


Day 2
RNA-seq workflow and analysis


Day 3
ChIP-seq workflow and analysis


Day 4
Data integration and reporting






What students will build
Students do not clone a finished analysis repository or copy a hidden template.
Instead, each participant progressively creates their own GitHub repository containing:

a clear project structure
metadata tables
analysis scripts
selected reports
figures
workflow documentation

By the end of the workshop, each student should have:

A reproducible GitHub repository
A documented RNA-seq and/or ChIP-seq workflow
A short report summarizing the analysis

The assembly of this repository will be used to evaluate student progress.



Datasets
The workshop uses publicly available datasets derived from small bacterial genomes.
The main examples are based on Helicobacter pylori strain N6 datasets generated to study the HP1021 redox switch regulon under microaerophilic and aerobic growth conditions:

Helicobacter pylori RNA-seq: E-MTAB-13025
Helicobacter pylori ChIP-seq: E-MTAB-13026

These datasets are associated with the publication:
Noszka M. et al. “Profiling of the Helicobacter pylori redox switch HP1021 regulon using a multi-omics approach.” Nature Communications (2023).

Publication: PubMed Central and Nature
RNA-seq dataset: E-MTAB-13025
ChIP-seq dataset: E-MTAB-13026

The full study includes multiple conditions and analyses. In this workshop, we focus on a small teaching subset of the wild-type strain under microaerobic and aerobic conditions.
Our small teaching workflow captures the logic of the published analysis, but it is simplified for laptop-scale execution. It should not be interpreted as a full reproduction of the paper.



Before you start
If this is your first visit, begin with:
Day 0 - Setup and readiness
Then continue through the lessons in sequence using the navigation panel on the left. Each day page will be released as the corresponding lesson becomes available.



Repository
Source repository:
https://github.com/fgualdr/reproducible-ngs-workshop
Citation information is available in CITATION.cff.



Questions and issue reporting
Questions, problems, or suggestions should preferably be reported through the GitHub repository issue tracker. This makes the discussion visible, traceable, and useful for other participants who may encounter the same problem.
Repository issues: https://github.com/fgualdr/reproducible-ngs-workshop/issues
For questions that are not suitable for a public issue, you can also contact:
francesco.gualdrini@gmail.com

title: Git and GitHub
text: Git tracks the analysis logic: README notes, scripts, metadata tables, configuration, logs, and small final result tables. GitHub provides remote backup, collaboration, and submission infrastructure.

title: Git and GitHub
text: Git tracks the analysis logic: README notes, scripts, metadata tables, configuration, logs, and small final result tables. GitHub provides remote backup, collaboration, and submission infrastructure.

title: Git and GitHub
text:
What to version

README and workflow notes.
Sample metadata and accession tables.
Scripts and command notes under scripts/.
Configuration files.
Small summary tables and final figures.

title: Git and GitHub
text:
What not to version

FASTQ, BAM, BAI, CRAM, SRA, bigWig, large archives, temporary files, and tool caches.
Passwords, tokens, unpublished private data, or confidential student information.

title: Git and GitHub
text:
Minimal commands
git init
git status
git add README.md .gitignore raw_data/metadata reference_genome scripts results/logs
git commit -m "Initialize reproducible NGS project"
git remote add origin git@github.com:USERNAME/PROJECT.git
git push -u origin main

title: Git and GitHub
text:
Commit checkpoints
Use small commits after meaningful stages: structure, metadata, retrieval plan, reference, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, integration, and final slides.
